title: The women in the garden
hook: the women are sent to charm him, and he stays unmoved (Buddhacarita 4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sick and the dead, death, and your line: the world goes gray. Did you stay a breath longer with something hard? Today the king tries one more remedy. Day seven hundred three.

The king has heard. His son came home from the road shaken, and now he won't stop thinking about old age and death. So the king reaches for the tool he trusts. He sends the prince to a beautiful garden outside the city, and he sends the women of the court with him. Their task is plain: delight him. Bring him back to the life of pleasure. Make him forget what he saw. Music under the trees. Flowers. Laughter by the water. The poem spends a long time in this garden, and every line of it is built to pull a young man's attention away from one thought.
screen: `THE KING TRIES AGAIN.` → `A GARDEN, MUSIC, THE COURT'S WOMEN.` → `MAKE HIM FORGET.`

segments.voice: First, the women. It matters how the poem sets this up. They didn't choose this. They were sent, by a king, with a task. At first, the poem says, they hold back, shy before the prince. Then they're urged on, and they do what they were told. They sing and dance, they tease and whisper, they wander close in the flowering garden. The poet describes it all at length, with the color and play of court poetry. Second, the prince. He doesn't scold them. He doesn't run. In the poem he simply isn't moved. He looks at the young women, bright and laughing, and what he sees is what the road just taught him: this beauty will age, these bodies will sicken, these lives will end. He's not cold toward them. He's thinking about them more truly than the garden wants him to. Third, the word itself. Unmoved doesn't mean frozen, or proud, or disgusted. In the Anguttara Nikaya the Buddha names eight worldly conditions, gain and loss, good name and bad name, praise and blame, pleasure and pain, and describes a mind they don't overturn. In the garden only the pleasant half is pulling, and steadiness looks like quiet. And fourth, the cost to the king. Another remedy has failed. The music played, the garden bloomed, and his son came home thinking the same thought. The poem doesn't blame anyone in the garden. The women did what they were asked. The prince did what he couldn't help. And the garden isn't finished with him yet. Before he goes home, a friend will try.
screen: `SENT, NOT CHOOSING.` · `HE SEES WHAT THE ROAD TAUGHT HIM.` · `UNMOVED IS NOT COLD.` · `THE KING'S REMEDY FAILS.` · then, large: `UNMOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one charm you can resist. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that pulls at you during an ordinary day. The phone face-down on the table. A snack you're not hungry for. A show that starts the next episode on its own. Pick one, and picture it in front of you now. Feel the pull, honestly, without pretending it isn't there. Then breathe, and let the pull rise and pass without obeying it. You're not fighting it. You're just not moved. The bell holds the time.
steadiness. What the prince shows when the court women are sent to charm him in the garden: courteous, unmoved, already thinking of age and death beneath the beauty. Today's word.
Your line: unmoved. Once today, when something built to grab you starts pulling, take one breath first, and see if you can stay upright and kind at the same time. Day seven hundred three.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers use the garden scene when speaking about sense pleasures and restraint, and in temple murals the prince is sometimes shown seated calmly among dancers and musicians.

myth: in the poem, the women set out to trap the prince on their own
the king sends them with a task.
the prince scolds the women and leaves
he stays, courteous and unmoved, thinking of age and death.
the garden blooms and the music plays, and the prince comes home with the same thought.

fork.setup: you're the prince, in a flowering garden, surrounded by music and laughter meant to make you forget the road. what do you do?
options: give in and forget what you saw.
stay where you are, courteous, and keep seeing clearly.
shout at everyone and storm home.
fork.reveal: he stays unmoved. not cold, not angry: he sees the beauty and also where it ends.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prince who didn't like parties.
what it means: he isn't cold toward the women; what he saw on the road keeps him steady in the garden.
what a scholar hears: the canto is written with the lush detail of court poetry, so the reader feels the pull the prince is resisting.
recall: the invitation at the rains' end

notes: All Buddhacarita material paraphrased (Cowell 1894 not on the validator list).
The scene is sensual in the original; the script keeps descriptions general and frames the women as sent and blameless. Keeper to confirm the framing.
Confirm in Cowell canto 4: the women's initial shyness before the prince, the urging (by Udayin, whose speech is tomorrow's lesson), and the prince's reflection on age and death while unmoved.
'Buddhist teaching speaks of steadiness' is general; the eight worldly winds (AN 8.6) could be cited here if wanted.
howItsDone's mural description is general; confirm or cut.
